M.title_en: Square Rank Badge for a Sixth-Rank Civil Official: Egret, Lotus Pond and Auspicious Clouds in Gauze Embroidery
M.introduction_en: A Ming-dynasty square rank badge for a sixth-rank civil official. This page gathers the museum record, visual observations, institutional background, craft information and unresolved questions.

overview.body_en:
This page gathers the museum record, visual observations, historical background, craft information and unresolved questions for this object. Open the sections below to read them. The regulations and comparative studies cited here explain the period; unless there is direct evidence, they should not be treated as this object's own documented history.

As you read, keep six kinds of information apart: museum record, visual observation, historical regulations, comparative research, possible interpretation, and unknown information.

M01.body_en:
This object is registered as 2024.CH-HKPM.6 under the name “Square Rank Badge with Egret, Lotus Pond and Auspicious Clouds in Gauze Embroidery, Sixth-Rank Civil Official”, dated to the Ming dynasty (1368–1644). “Sixth-rank civil official”, “egret” and “gauze embroidery” in the record all refer to this particular object. The record does not contain material that would fix the exact year of making, the craftspeople, or the original wearer.

Square rank badge (fangbu): a square garment insignia with a recognisable pattern, attached to or integrated into an official robe. In the registration photograph, white birds, dense flowers and plants, water scenes and auspicious clouds can be identified.

M02.title_en: M02 · Close looking: egret, lotus pond and pattern structure
M02.body_en:
Fig. M-1 | Upper bird motif and surrounding patterns | Fig. M-2 | Detail of egret, water and plants

Fig. M-3 | Position of the egret and lotus pond | Fig. M-4 | Detail of flowers, plants and bird

In the overall composition, white egrets are interwoven with lotus, plants and water inside a square decorative field.

Two kinds of information can be separated: the motifs already identified in the registered name, and the birds, flowers, water and their relative positions that are directly visible.

Detail 1 shows the relation between the upper bird and the plant pattern; details 2 and 3 allow the bird and the water to be compared; detail 4 shows the clustering of flowers and the layering of plants.

Unlike images that show a single bird, this badge has a rich lotus-pond background. Reading it means attending both to the central status marker and to the surrounding natural imagery, which may carry different cultural meanings.

M03.title_en: M03 · Meaning in the Ming dress regulations
M03.body_en:
Evidence level: historical regulations | historical interpretation    References: [MING-01] [MING-02] [ACAD-01]

Through its dress regulations, the Ming state turned official rank into a visible garment code. In the twenty-fourth year of the Hongwu reign (1391), under Emperor Taizu (Zhu Yuanzhang), patterns on everyday robes were tied to categories and grades of office. Later compilations — juan 58 of the Ming Huidian and juan 67 of the Ming Shi — preserve correspondences such as the white pheasant for fifth-rank civil officials and the egret for sixth rank.

Such bird patterns did more than decorate a robe: they linked image, statutory rank and social recognition. A wearer did not need his name written on the robe, and people who knew the code could read category and grade from the pattern. The pattern cannot, however, tell us an individual official's name, native place, postings or career.

The common summary that civil officials used birds and military officials beasts is broadly right, but the actual regulations included specific functions and changed over time. The Ming Huidian is a later compiled statute book: its record of Hongwu practice is relevant evidence, but it does not mean this badge was made when the book was compiled, and 1391, the year of the regulation, is not the exact year this badge was made.

M04.title_en: M04 · Cultural meanings: rank symbol and lotus pond
M04.body_en:
Evidence level: institutional fact | comparative motif study | unresolved    References: [MING-01] [MUSEUM-04] [HKPM-P]

The egret on this badge has a clear role as a status marker in the Ming civil-rank system, and that institutional meaning can be discussed from the statutes. The lotus and lotus-pond imagery can also be read within the longer tradition of flower-and-bird and auspicious patterns. That does not make the lotus pond a statutory rank image for any grade.

The Hong Kong Palace Museum's general educational material on patterns notes that egret, reed and lotus can, in some combinations, evoke puns about official careers, examinations or good wishes.

M05.title_en: M05 · Craft: from gauze ground to coloured embroidery
M05.body_en:
Evidence level: museum craft term | general craft research    References: [HKPM-P] [ACAD-06] [ACAD-01]

“Gauze embroidery” (shaxiu) in the registered name covers two steps: sha, a gauze ground that has already been woven, and xiu, embroidery worked into that ground with threads to form birds, flowers and clouds.

The general sequence can be read as: prepare silk or gauze threads → weave the gauze ground → fix the pattern layout → embroider the ground → combine it with the garment.

Gauze and satin are different ground structures with different surfaces. Gauze is usually more open and porous; satin looks smoother and glossier because of its longer floats. Both can be embroidered. “Gauze embroidery” is therefore neither embroidery on a satin ground nor a complex pattern woven in one pass on a loom, and it differs from painting or printing.

Research on surviving objects also shows that Ming rank badges were not attached to robes in only one way: some were designed together with the garment fabric, while others were made separately and then sewn onto the robe.

M06.body_en:
Evidence level: historical weaving regulations | comparative research | unknown for this object    References: [MING-04] [ACAD-06] [ACAD-01]

Ming silk production included both state-run weaving and dyeing offices and private production in many regions. Juan 201 of the Revised Ming Huidian records the weaving and dyeing bureaux of the two capitals, related supply channels and the division of work between institutions; Nanjing, Suzhou and Hangzhou were important historical silk-producing centres, and the Jiangnan region also had extensive private weaving and embroidery. This institutional and production network explains the social and technical environment in which official dress textiles could be made.

The existence of state weaving bureaux does not mean that every official's rank badge was made by a particular imperial workshop. Historical sources can show that “the Ming state had such offices and duties”; they cannot show that object 2024.CH-HKPM.6 came from one specific workshop or bureau, and the fact that a similar egret badge was made somewhere does not mean this badge came from the same place.

For this object, “the existence of state and private weaving networks in the Ming” is historical background, while “which embroiderer and which workshop made this badge” remains unknown.

M07.title_en: M07 · Historical setting: how a bird became a language of status
M07.body_en:
Evidence level: teaching scenario built on the regulations | not a biography of this object    References: [MING-01] [MING-02] [ACAD-01]

Imagine a public occasion in the Ming, with an official wearing an everyday robe bearing a bird pattern. People familiar with the dress code might infer his rank from the image; to viewers who did not know the code, it would simply be a beautiful flower-and-bird picture. Because the regulations tied specific birds to ranks, the same piece of silk carried both an aesthetic and a visible status function.

This badge also connects to another historical thread: the relation between silk weaving, embroidery craftspeople, garment administration and the officials who wore the robes. Regulations assigned rank meanings to patterns, but putting a pattern onto a garment still required raw materials, dyeing and weaving, embroidery and garment making. A single surviving badge lets us enter the world of Ming institutions and craft through one small surface of clothing.

M08.body_en:
Evidence level: unknown information | further research    References: [HKPM-P] [ACAD-01]

The available material cannot establish the exact year this badge was made, nor the original wearer, the craftspeople, the person who ordered it, the original workshop or the place of production. A single image also cannot show whether it sat on the front or the back of a robe, whether it was once part of a pair, or whether it was cut down.

Precise dimensions, material analysis, a specific gauze structure, stitch analysis and dye reports are all missing. The registered terms “egret” and “lotus pond” have object-based support, but whether the plants shown actually form a specific punning motif, and why the designer chose them, still need verification.

Not knowing is not the same as being unable to interpret. Historical research can present the institutions and craft background that are documented, together with comparative interpretations that have support, while marking clearly what cannot yet be settled. The more specific a claim about this object is, the more it needs evidence from this object itself.

T.title_en: Tang-Dynasty Brocade with Paired Griffins in Pearl Roundels on a Red Ground
T.introduction_en: A Tang-dynasty fragment of brocade with paired griffins in pearl roundels. This page gathers the museum record, visual observations, Silk Road background, craft information and unresolved questions.

overview.body_en:
This page gathers the museum record, visual observations, historical background, craft information and unresolved questions for this object. Open the sections below to read them. The regulations and comparative studies cited here explain the period; unless there is direct evidence, they should not be treated as this object's own documented history.

As you read, keep six kinds of information apart: museum record, visual observation, historical regulations, comparative research, possible interpretation, and unknown information.

T01.body_en:
Evidence level: museum record | visual observation    References: [P1]

This object is numbered 2024.CH-HKPM.2 and registered internally as “Brocade with Paired Griffins in Pearl Roundels on a Red Ground” (shortened in teaching material to “Tang red-ground brocade with paired griffins in roundels”). It is dated to the seventh to eighth century, Tang dynasty, and is a fragment of silk brocade. The registered name records the red ground, the pearl roundels and the paired, facing griffins.

“Griffin” names the type of fantastic animal in the image; the name itself does not show that the textile belonged to a specific religious rite, nor does it establish which region it came from. Registering the object as “brocade” describes its collection category only; it does not establish a specific warp-faced or weft-faced structure, a twill weave, or a loom type.

T02.title_en: T02 · Close looking: pearl roundels and facing animals
T02.body_en:
Evidence level: visual observation | pattern-structure analysis    References: [P1]

Fig. T-1 | Detail of a pearl roundel at the left | Fig. T-2 | Central roundel with facing animals

Fig. T-3 | Repeated pattern and textile edge at the right | Fig. T-4 | Detail of the pearl border

Fig. T-5 | Animal and central axis inside a roundel

The composition can be read on three levels. The first is the circular frame made of pearl dots — the pearl roundel, or medallion border. The second is the pair of griffins inside the roundel, facing each other. The third is the repetition of similar roundels across the fabric, creating a continuous rhythm.

A single roundel can be treated as a relatively complete visual unit: the border organises the central image, the two animals create a symmetrical relation, and the unit is repeated to produce a wider continuous pattern. Reading “border — central animal — repeated unit” together explains the decorative structure better than remembering only that there are two animals.

T03.title_en: T03 · Images on the move along Tang trade routes
T03.body_en:
Evidence level: comparative research | historical exchange background    References: [R1] [R2] [R4] [R5]

The development of Tang silk patterns is connected with the movement of goods, the activity of craftspeople and the exchange of images between China, Central Asia and West Asia. Pearl roundels and paired animals appear on silks from several regions; comparable museum objects help us compare these layouts, and some studies discuss the influence of late Sasanian and Sogdian image traditions.

Related textiles in other museums, for example, show animals inside pearl rings, and some of these pieces have documented provenance or technical records. They show that the motif type was not confined to one region: motifs could travel with merchants, gifts, textiles and craftspeople, and be recombined in new places.

Cultural exchange is not the same as copying. A region that borrowed a border or a facing-animal structure might change details, uses and meanings. Visual similarity can be a clue for investigating exchange, but it cannot by itself assign two textiles to the same craftsperson, workshop, year or place of production.

When discussing this object, “it belongs to a transregional tradition of pearl roundels with paired animals” must therefore be kept strictly separate from “this brocade was certainly made in a specific Sasanian or Sogdian workshop”. The second claim lacks direct evidence from this object.

T04.title_en: T04 · Griffin imagery and its reinterpretation
T04.body_en:
Evidence level: image naming | comparative research | contextual interpretation    References: [P1] [R1] [R5]

The registration calls the paired animals griffins, also commonly rendered as lion-griffins. Griffin-like images exist in West Asian, Central Asian and other traditions, but “seeing a griffin” does not mean we know this textile's ritual use, the wearer's beliefs or a single symbolic meaning.

In transregional image exchange, the same animal motif could be borrowed, redrawn and recombined into new pattern units, acquiring new explanations in different cultural settings. Discussing a specific original meaning requires evidence from this textile, a sufficiently close historical context, excavated material, contemporary images or texts — not simply the name of the animal.

T05.title_en: T05 · Craft: brocade and weaving technology
T05.body_en:
Evidence level: museum record | comparison with related craft    References: [P1] [R1] [R3]

“Brocade” is this object's registered category; complex polychrome patterns require organised arrangement of different silk threads and repeated pattern units. The name “brocade” and a photograph of the front, however, cannot establish which warp-and-weft structure was used, and a visually complex pattern is not by itself evidence of a twill weft-faced brocade.

Research on comparable Tang silks concerns weft-faced patterning and twill weft-faced brocade, and some scholars and museums describe the exchange between Central Asian weft-patterning techniques and Chinese technology around the early seventh century. Weft patterning can help explain how some complex polychrome silks were made, but that is a conclusion from the technical history of the period and from other objects.

A similar brocade with paired lions in pearl roundels in the National Palace Museum, Taipei, has been described in research as a twill weft-faced brocade. It helps us understand the techniques such textiles may have used, but its technical findings cannot simply be transferred to 2024.CH-HKPM.2. Confirming the structure of this piece would require examination of the reverse, microscopic study of the warp and weft, and the museum's technical records.

Unlike the Ming badge, where embroidery was worked on a gauze ground, the complex patterns of a brocade are usually formed by the weave itself; not every patterned silk should be described loosely as embroidery.

T06.body_en:
Evidence level: historical research | possible routes | unknown for this object    References: [R4] [R5] [R6] [P1]

The spread of silk technology in and around the Tang period involved merchants, craftspeople and regional weaving centres. Studies discuss Sogdian merchants and weavers in Central Asia, and the development of silk production and the re-creation of foreign patterns in areas such as Shu (Yizhou) and Turfan within China. Several regions may historically have been able to make or transmit such patterns; this must not be misread as meaning that all comparable brocades came from one place.

Modern scholarship contains references to Dou Shilun supervising pattern design for brocades in Tang Yizhou, which can be used to introduce Tang pattern design and local weaving; the classical sources cited in this material, however, are quoted through modern studies, were not collated line by line against the originals, and none of them links Dou Shilun directly to this griffin brocade.

This piece lacks an archaeological record that would independently identify its place of production, a workshop signature, or a technical report on its structure. It cannot be called the product of a particular Persian workshop merely because the griffin resembles Sasanian or Sogdian traditions, nor attributed to a Chengdu workshop merely because Tang Shu brocade was famous.

T07.title_en: T07 · Historical setting: how patterns cross cultures
T07.body_en:
Evidence level: teaching scenario built on historical background | not this object's provenance chain    References: [R1] [R2] [R5]

Imagine a traveller familiar with textiles seeing pearl rings and paired animals in different regions: on one cloth the two animals inside a roundel face each other; on another the animals have changed, but the ring and the repetition are still recognisable. The story helps explain how patterns are transmitted, imitated and redesigned.

The trade in silks moved finished objects, but could also involve weavers, dyeing and weaving knowledge, and ideas about composition. Sometimes the form was kept while details and meanings changed in a new region. Pearl roundels are a good case for observing this kind of “partial continuity and reorganisation”.

T08.body_en:
Evidence level: unknown information | to be investigated    References: [P1] [R3] [R5]

The existing record does not establish the original workshop, findspot, exact country or region of production, or maker of this piece, and there are no object-level technical results that independently determine its warp-and-weft structure, loom, dye recipe or fibre composition.

Magnified details help us see the repeated pattern but are not microscopic structural evidence; reports that other Tang brocades are twill weft-faced, or studies of Sasanian and Sogdian imagery, do not mean this brocade has the same origin, structure or use.

Further work would need to check dimensions, the reverse of the fabric, warp-and-weft records, dye and fibre analysis, old collection history, transfers of ownership and conservation history. The griffin image here has a clear name and observable form; its specific original religious meaning or social function remains unconfirmed for this piece.
